Table: Stages of pressure ulcer

 


Stage 1: Stage one pressure ulcers are characterized by erythema of intact skin that does not blanch when pressed upon. The skin may appear red and feel warm when touched.


Stage 2: Stage two pressure ulcers involve partial thickness skin loss involving epidermis, dermis, or both. The lesion is superficial and presents clinically as an abrasion, blister, or shallow center. It may be red in color and feel warm when touched.


Stage 3: Stage three decubitus ulcers are full thickness skin loss involving damage or necrosis of subcutaneous tissue (the tissue below the skin) that may extend down to, but not through, underlying fascia. The sore presents clinically as a deep crater with or without undermining of adjacent tissue. The area surrounding the sore may be red and hard, and warmth may be palpated throughout.


Stage 4: The stage four pressure ulcer presents as full thickness skin loss with extensive destruction, tissue necrosis, or damage to muscle, bone, or supporting structures. This is the most severe of pressure ulcer formation and is most difficult to treat. In stage four ulcers, there may be a deep crater in the sore with significant drainage and pus. A foul odor may be present, and the tissue surrounding the area may be dark purple or black.

• Major burn injuries result in an area of necrotic zone, beneath this lies the zone of stasis and results in release of inflammatory mediators which increase the capillary permeability and lead to localized burn wound edema. Inflammatory and vasoactive mediators are responsible for local vasoconstriction, systemic vasodilation and increased transcapillary permeability. Increase in permeability results in a rapid transfer of water, inorganic solutes and plasma proteins between the intravascular and interstitial spaces. It is well-documented that fluid is lost from the circulation into burned tissue because of a moderate increase in capillary permeability to fluid and macromolecules and a modest increase in hydrostatic pressure inside the perfusing micro vessels. Subsequently, intravascular hypovolemia and hemoconcentration develop and maximum levels are reached within 12 hours after injury. The steady intravascular fluid loss due to these sequences of events requires sustained replacement of intravascular volume in order to prevent end-organ hypoperfusion and ischemia.

• Trendelenburg test is used to assess varicose vein. The test is performed initially by draining the superficial lower extremity veins by elevating the lower limbs to 45° and gently stroking the limb from the foot along the course of the major veins. A tourniquet is then placed as close to the groin as possible and applied tightly enough to prevent superficial vein reflux. The patient is asked to stand and the limb is examined. If the distal veins remain collapsed for 15 to 30 seconds after standing, the tourniquet is released.
  • Saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) incompetence is diagnosed, if the distal veins fill rapidly upon release of the tourniquet.
  • If the caudal veins fill rapidly when the patient stands with the tourniquet in place, perforator incompetence is suggested.
  • The location of the incompetent perforator can then be determined by varying the position of the tourniquet. Rapid filling of the varices with a tourniquet in the suprapatellar position can identify an incompetent midthigh perforator, and rapid filling with the tourniquet below the knee suggests incompetent lower leg perforators.

    1. Make the child sit upright in a comfortable position, slightly leaning forward.
    2. Squeeze the lower, soft part of the nose with the fingers, a tissue or a cloth for ten minutes.
    3. Apply an ‘icepack’ or a cool, wet cloth to the bridge (top) of child’s nose.
    4. Encourage child to spit out any blood it has in its mouth and not to swallow it.
    5. Do not keep checking whether the bleeding has stopped by removing your fingers. The blood needs to clot and this takes time.
    6. Release the nose and check if the bleeding has stopped (if the nosebleed continues repeat the process for another ten minutes).
    7. Once the bleeding has stopped, make sure the child does not pick or blow its nose for 24 hours.
    8. Child should not run around or play ‘rough’ for two hours after the nosebleed, to prevent it from bleeding again.
  • Supine and Trendelenburg positions are not recommended as there is no scientific evidence that they prevent nose bleeding.

Figure: Position of child in nose bleeding

Leaning backward while sitting may cause blood and nasal discharge to enter the stomach causing gastric upset and vomiting.

·         Injury to Brachial plexus can cause paralysis of arm and loss of sensation and not foot drop as it innervates muscles and skin of the whole arm but not foot.

• Candidiasis is a fungal infection caused by any type of candida (yeast). It is commonly called oral thrush when it affects mouth having white patches of tongue, mouth and throat. It is having common symptoms, like soreness and itching in the vagina, vaginal discharge, pain during sex, white patches on vagina, it can also affect the foot called athlete’s foot. A white discharge, especially at the beginning or end of the menstrual cycle, is normal. But, if the discharge is accompanied by itching and has a thick, cottage cheese-like consistency or appearance, it’s not normal. Type of discharge may be a sign of yeast infection that is candidiasis.
  • Trichomoniasis is a parasitic infection caused by Trichomonas It leads to vaginitis and vaginal discharge, itching, bad smell from vagina, etc.Trichomoniasis results in a yellow or green discharge that has a foul odor.
  • Syphilis is mainly a sexually transmitted infection caused by bacterium Treponema pallidum. It is mainly spread by sexual activity and may also be transmitted from mother to baby during pregnancy or at birth.
  • Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhea. It includes the symptoms in men like burning urination, discharge from penis, red and swollen penis opening, tender testicles, and sore throat, and in women burning urination, vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain and inflammation. Gonorrhea produces an abnormal discharge; it is often yellow, greenish or cloudy in color.

choices.correct_explanation:
• Transfer of frustration due to unmet goals to another person or weaker subject is known as displacement. For example, Mr. Raju is frustrated at his workplace but unable to show his impulse to his Boss. He comes to home and shouts at his child or wife, who is weaker, objects for Mr. Raju.
  • Projection is a form of defense mechanism in which unwanted feelings are displaced onto another person. Mr. Raju hates his colleagues at workplace but instead of accepting this, he projects that his colleagues hate him.
  • Rationalization is a defense mechanism that involves the justification of an unacceptable behavior, thought or feelingin a logical manner, avoiding the true reason for the action.
  • Regressionis a psychological defense mechanism in which a person abandons age-appropriate coping strategies in favor of earlier, more childlike patterns of behavior.
